issue: Which constitutional provision supplies a criminal defendant's right to be present at sentencing: the Due Process Clause or the Confrontation Clause?
provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause); U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause); FED. R. CRIM. P. 32(i)(2)

sides.position: The right to be present at sentencing derives from the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
cases: United States v. Diggles, 957 F.3d 551 (5th Cir. 2020) (en banc)
United States v. Montoya, 82 F.4th 640 (9th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: The right to be present at sentencing derives from the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment.
cases: United States v. Ferrario-Pozzi, 368 F.3d 5 (1st Cir. 2004)
United States v. Townsend, 33 F.3d 1230 (10th Cir. 1994)

this_court: Due Process Clause for proceedings lacking testimony, which includes most sentencings; the Confrontation Clause may also apply in the rare sentencing proceedings that include evidence or witness testimony.
quote: The Supreme Court has not directly addressed the constitutional basis for a defendant’s right to be present during sentencing, and the circuits are split on the basis for this right.
cite: United States v. Cynthia Montoya, 82 F.4th 640 (9th Cir. 2023)
